questions.question: Which classical GoF design patterns are still worth knowing in modern Java (21+), and which have been superseded by language features, dependency injection, or functional/reactive idioms?
questions.title: GoF Patterns vs Modern Java: Strategy vs Lambdas, Singleton vs DI, Factory vs Builder, Observer vs Reactive, Command vs Events
questions.direct_answer: **Most GoF patterns still matter, but their expression has changed.** Modern Java makes many of them one-liners: **Strategy** is a `Function`/lambda, **Command** is a `Runnable` or record + handler, **Template Method** is `List<Step>`, **Iterator** is built-in. Others shift purpose: **Singleton** is replaced by DI scopes (Spring's `@Singleton`/default scope) in 90% of cases, **Factory** is often just a builder + static method or a `Supplier`, **Observer** is replaced by reactive streams (`Flux`, `Flow`) or messaging. Some are more relevant than ever: **Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Builder, Visitor** (with sealed types), **Chain of Responsibility** (e.g., Spring filters), and **State** (with sealed + records). Anti-patterns in modern code: Singletons as global mutable state, Factory-of-Factory-of-Factory pyramids, Observer with leaky listener lists, Template Method inheritance trees. The senior takeaway: **know the patterns by name so you can recognize them in code, frameworks, and design conversations** — but reach for the **simplest modern idiom** first (function, record, sealed type, DI), and introduce explicit patterns only when complexity justifies the ceremony.

interviewer_intent.soft_skills: Pragmatism, historical context, ability to judge when patterns help vs. hurt, language fluency
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting GoF gospel; over-applying patterns to simple code; ignoring that DI+records+sealed fundamentally changed the landscape
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map classical patterns to modern idioms; recognize anti-patterns; know when ceremony helps; reference Spring/Java stdlib examples

sections.title: Why Compare Patterns to Modern Idioms
sections.content:
The GoF *Design Patterns* (1994) emerged in a world of Smalltalk, C++, and Java 1.0 — no lambdas, no DI frameworks, no generics, no records, no sealed types, no reactive streams. Many patterns were workarounds for **missing language features**. Once the language or framework provides a better abstraction, re-implementing the pattern by hand is ceremony, not engineering.

**What's changed since 1994**
- **Lambdas (Java 8)** killed most Strategy/Command boilerplate
- **Streams + functional interfaces** replaced many Iterator / Template patterns
- **Dependency Injection (Spring)** replaced most Singleton/Factory uses
- **Records (Java 16)** made immutable value objects trivial — a big chunk of Builder use cases
- **Sealed types + pattern matching (Java 17/21)** enabled safer State/Visitor alternatives
- **CompletableFuture / Reactive Streams** replaced most Observer
- **Event systems (Kafka, Spring events)** replaced Mediator/Observer at architectural scale
- **Modules (JPMS) + visibility** reduced the need for Facade ceremony

**What hasn't changed**
- The **vocabulary** — saying "this is a Strategy" is still faster than explaining it
- The **problems** — coupling, variation, extensibility, testability are eternal
- Many patterns are **still the right answer**, just expressed more simply

**Senior perspective**
- Know patterns to recognize them, not to evangelize them
- Reach for the simplest idiom first; introduce explicit pattern when complexity demands it
- Be suspicious of pattern-heavy code — it often signals over-engineering

sections.title: Patterns Largely Replaced by Language Features
sections.content:
**Strategy → Function / Lambda**
- GoF: an interface `SortStrategy` with subclass per algorithm
- Modern: `Comparator<User>` via `Comparator.comparing(User::getAge)` — one line
- When Strategy is still explicit: state-bearing strategies, discovery via DI, runtime swapping with names (named beans)
- Use Strategy when you need a registry/catalog; use a lambda otherwise

**Command → Runnable / Record + Handler**
- GoF: `Command.execute()` interface
- Modern: `Runnable` for no-arg; record + handler for richer commands; CQRS uses records as commands
- Example: `record CreateOrder(UUID userId, List<Item> items)` + `CommandHandler<CreateOrder>`
- Still valuable when commands need serialization, queueing, undo/redo, auditing

**Template Method → List of Steps / Function composition**
- GoF: abstract class with hooks; subclass overrides
- Modern: pipeline — `List<Function<Ctx, Ctx>>` or Spring Batch `Step`s
- Inheritance trees were a common Template Method anti-pattern; composition wins
- Reach for Template Method when algorithmic skeleton is truly stable and hooks are well-known

**Iterator → Built-in + Streams**
- GoF: explicit `Iterator<T>` custom implementations
- Modern: `Iterable<T>` + for-each, or `Stream<T>` for chaining
- Custom iterators still useful for generators, infinite sequences, external state

**Observer → Reactive / Events / Messaging**
- GoF: `Subject` with `List<Observer>`; manual subscribe/unsubscribe; leaky and thread-unsafe
- Modern: Reactor `Flux`, Java 9 `Flow`, RxJava; or Spring events (`@EventListener`); or Kafka/SQS at system scale
- Built-in backpressure, thread safety, lifecycle management
- Manual Observer only for very small, local callbacks (and even then, consider `Consumer<T>`)

**Singleton → DI scope**
- GoF: private static instance, private constructor
- Modern: Spring `@Component` default singleton scope, managed lifecycle, testable via replacement
- Manual singleton still valid for utility classes (`java.util.Objects`), but mostly avoided for business code
- Anti-pattern: Singleton as global mutable state — makes testing painful, threading ambiguous

**Factory Method → Supplier / static factory / Builder**
- GoF: parallel class hierarchies for factories
- Modern: `Supplier<T>`, `Optional.of()`, `List.of()`, `Map.of()`, static `create()` methods
- Spring `@Bean` methods are factories managed by DI
- Factory still useful for complex construction with discovery (e.g., `ServiceLoader`, Spring conditional beans)

sections.title: Patterns Still Very Relevant (Even Improved)
sections.content:
**Adapter**
- Translating one interface to another — still a real, common problem
- JDBC to JPA, old SDK to new interface, third-party API to domain port
- Java's first-class interfaces keep this clean; often implemented as a thin wrapper class

**Decorator**
- Wrap an object to add behavior transparently
- `BufferedReader(new FileReader(...))` — textbook decoration in the JDK
- Modern variant: functional decoration with HOFs (`Function.andThen`), Spring AOP, servlet filters, HandlerInterceptors
- Excellent for cross-cutting: logging, caching, retry, rate limiting

**Facade**
- Simplifying a complex subsystem with a single entry point
- Every well-designed service interface is effectively a Facade
- Spring's `JdbcTemplate` facades JDBC's cruft
- Value: reduces cognitive load and coupling for clients

**Builder**
- For immutable objects with many fields
- Lombok `@Builder`, or manual nested builders
- Records handle the simple case; Builder wins for 10+ fields, optional fields, validation
- Great for DSL-like construction: `QueryBuilder`, `HttpRequest.newBuilder()`

**Chain of Responsibility**
- Ordered handlers where each can process or pass on
- Spring Security filter chain, Servlet filters, Netty pipelines are canonical examples
- Clean, testable, dynamically composable

**Visitor (with sealed types)**
- Add operations to a closed type hierarchy without modifying the hierarchy
- Java 21: sealed types + pattern matching make this elegant
- Example: AST nodes with sealed `Node`; `switch(node) { case Add a -> ...; case Mul m -> ... }`
- Traditional double-dispatch Visitor is now an anti-pattern — pattern matching is simpler and exhaustive-checked

**State (with sealed + records)**
- Object changes behavior based on state
- Sealed state type + pattern matching transitions
- Example: `sealed interface OrderState permits Created, Paid, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled`
- Transitions as pure functions returning new states
- Immutable, testable, exhaustive

**Composite**
- Tree of same-interface objects (single item + collection treated uniformly)
- File system nodes, UI components, report aggregators
- Still useful; sealed types make it safer

**Mediator**
- Centralize complex communication between objects
- At system scale: event bus, Kafka, message broker
- At class scale: Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher`
- Avoids N² coupling

sections.title: Anti-Pattern Warning Signs
sections.content:
Patterns can turn into anti-patterns when applied without judgment.

**Singleton abuse**
- Global mutable state; untestable; threading nightmare
- Hidden dependencies; `SomethingManager.getInstance()` everywhere
- Replace with DI; if legacy, wrap behind an interface you can mock

**Factory pyramids**
- `AbstractBeanFactoryFactoryProvider` — real code, really bad
- Usually sign of over-architected test double; a plain method or `Supplier` suffices

**Observer lists that leak**
- Manual subscribe/unsubscribe; forgotten unsubscribe → memory leak or stale callbacks
- Use reactive or event systems with explicit lifecycle

**Template Method inheritance trees**
- 5-level deep abstract class hierarchy for "variation"
- Brittle: changing a step breaks all subclasses in non-obvious ways
- Replace with composition: list of steps, function pipeline, visitor on sealed state

**Visitor double-dispatch boilerplate**
- Pre-sealed, Visitor required `accept(visitor)` per class
- Modern Java: `switch` with pattern matching, exhaustiveness-checked

**Decorator stack 10 deep**
- Wrapping 10 times is hard to reason about; reflect carefully
- Consider a single pipeline abstraction or AOP when cross-cutting is the real intent

**Builder for 2-field objects**
- Overkill; use a constructor or record
- Builder earns its keep at 5+ fields with optional/validated ones

**Facade that doesn't simplify**
- Just forwards 1:1 to an internal API — adds layer, no value
- Facade should genuinely reduce surface area

**Pattern-named classes instead of domain-named**
- `UserFactoryFactory` tells you nothing; `UserFactory` is OK; `UserRegistration` is better
- Domain language over pattern terminology in naming

sections.title: Trade-offs and Decision Heuristics
sections.content:
**When to use a pattern vs. a simpler idiom**
- **One place, simple behavior** → lambda, record, function reference
- **Multiple implementations, registry, discovery** → explicit pattern (Strategy, Factory with DI)
- **Cross-cutting concern** → AOP, filter/interceptor chains (Chain of Responsibility variant), decorator
- **Complex state machine** → State + sealed types
- **Closed hierarchy + new operations** → Visitor via sealed + pattern matching

**When modern idioms are better**
- Reducing ceremony for simple variation → lambda/function
- Eliminating inheritance trees → composition
- Event delivery at scale → messaging
- Immutable value objects → records
- Dependency resolution → DI

**When classical patterns still win**
- Need to preserve commands (serialize, queue, audit, undo) → Command record + handler
- Complex object graphs construction → Builder
- Multiple adapters between APIs → Adapter with explicit interface
- Composable cross-cutting behavior → Decorator
- Policy swapping with discovery → Strategy as named beans

**Naming discipline**
- Prefer domain names: `ShippingPolicy`, not `ShippingStrategy`
- Pattern is an implementation detail; domain language stays stable as implementations evolve

**When to refactor away from a pattern**
- Pattern is present but variation never materialized → collapse to concrete
- Inheritance tree is deeper than 2 levels → often a pattern gone wrong
- Builder has one consumer with all required fields → collapse to constructor/record
- Observer has one subscriber that's always installed → direct call

**Cost of ceremony**
- Every layer of abstraction costs cognitive load and test surface
- "YAGNI" applies: add the pattern when variation is real, not speculative
- Refactor *to* a pattern when a second variation shows up, not before

**Teaching and review**
- In code review: prefer the simplest idiom that handles current and near-future variation
- Name the pattern when it helps communication: "let's make this a Strategy so we can plug in Risk Engine V2"
- Don't require pattern ceremony on every PR; that's cargo cult

**Language evolution keeps changing the answer**
- Records reduced Builder need significantly
- Sealed types + pattern matching changed State and Visitor
- Virtual threads may reduce some callback/observer patterns further
- Reassess every 3–5 years; don't cement 1994 answers into 2026 code

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Patterns are **vocabulary and tools**, not dogma — reach for the simplest idiom first
- **Largely replaced by language features**: Strategy, Command, Template Method, Iterator, Observer, Singleton, Factory Method
- **Still very relevant**: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Builder, Chain of Responsibility, Visitor (sealed), State (sealed), Composite, Mediator
- **Modern Java impact**: lambdas, records, sealed types + pattern matching, DI, reactive streams, modules
- **Anti-patterns**: Singleton as global state, factory pyramids, leaky Observer lists, deep Template Method inheritance, Builders for trivial objects
- **Name by domain**, not pattern — `ShippingPolicy`, not `ShippingStrategy`
- **Refactor to a pattern** when variation is real, not speculatively
- **Every abstraction costs** — cognitive load, tests, code to navigate
- **Reassess periodically** — language evolution changes the right answer every few years
- Senior value: recognize patterns in the wild, use them for communication, avoid pattern-dogma reviews

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Most GoF patterns still matter, but their expression has changed dramatically in modern Java. Patterns are vocabulary — you need to recognize them — but reach for the simplest modern idiom first.

**Largely replaced by language features**
- Strategy → Function / lambda / Comparator.comparing
- Command → Runnable or record + handler
- Template Method → list of steps or function pipeline
- Iterator → built-in Iterable and Stream
- Observer → Flux, Flow, RxJava, Spring events, Kafka
- Singleton → DI scope, Spring @Component default
- Factory Method → Supplier, static factory, List.of / Map.of, Spring @Bean

**Still very relevant and often improved**
- Adapter — translating interfaces is a real recurring problem
- Decorator — functional decoration, AOP, filters, interceptors
- Facade — simplifying complex subsystems; good service interfaces are facades
- Builder — 5+ fields, optional fields, validation; records cover simple case
- Chain of Responsibility — Spring Security filter chain, Netty pipelines
- Visitor — sealed types + pattern matching made it elegant and exhaustive
- State — sealed interface + records + pattern matching for transitions
- Composite — trees; sealed types make it safer
- Mediator — at scale: event bus, Kafka; at class scale: ApplicationEventPublisher

**Modern Java changes to notice**
- Lambdas killed most Strategy/Command boilerplate
- Records made immutable value objects trivial
- Sealed types + pattern matching enabled safer State/Visitor
- CompletableFuture and reactive streams replaced Observer
- DI replaced Singleton/Factory in 90% of cases
- Modules reduced Facade ceremony

**Anti-pattern warning signs**
- Singleton as global mutable state
- Factory pyramids like AbstractBeanFactoryFactoryProvider
- Observer lists that leak on forgotten unsubscribe
- Template Method inheritance trees 5 levels deep
- Visitor double-dispatch boilerplate where pattern matching would do
- Decorator stacks 10 deep
- Builders for 2-field objects
- Facades that just forward 1:1
- Pattern-named classes instead of domain-named

**Decision heuristics**
- One place, simple behavior → lambda / record / function ref
- Multiple implementations with discovery → explicit Strategy/Factory with DI
- Cross-cutting concern → AOP, filter chain, decorator
- Complex state machine → State + sealed types
- Closed hierarchy + new operations → Visitor via sealed + pattern match
- Commands need serialization/queueing/audit → Command record + handler
- Complex object construction → Builder

**Naming discipline**
- Prefer domain names: ShippingPolicy, not ShippingStrategy
- Pattern is implementation detail; domain language is stable

**When to refactor away**
- Pattern present but variation never materialized → collapse to concrete
- Inheritance tree deeper than 2 levels → often pattern gone wrong
- Builder with one consumer and all required fields → constructor/record
- Observer with one subscriber always installed → direct call

**Cost of ceremony**
- Each abstraction costs cognitive load, test surface, code to navigate
- YAGNI: add when variation is real, not speculative
- Refactor to pattern when second variation shows up

**Teaching and review**
- Simplest idiom for current and near-future variation
- Name the pattern when it helps communication
- Don't cargo-cult pattern ceremony on every PR

**Language keeps changing the answer**
- Records reduced Builder need
- Sealed + pattern matching changed State and Visitor
- Virtual threads may reduce some callback patterns further
- Reassess every 3–5 years; don't cement 1994 answers into 2026 code

**Bottom line**
- Patterns are a shared vocabulary and recognition tool
- Modern Java has absorbed many of them as features
- Know the classics; apply the simplest idiom; introduce explicit patterns only when complexity justifies the ceremony
